newsitem.title: USA: Clinton delivers eulogy at Brennan's funeral.
newsitem.headline: Clinton delivers eulogy at Brennan's funeral.

text.p: President Clinton delivered a moving eulogy Tuesday for William Brennan, calling the late Supreme Court justice a "legal giant" whose rulings helped reshape U.S. history.

"We recall him as a legal giant, the balance wheel who moulded the Supreme Court into an instrument of liberty and equality during tumultuous times," he said at a service also attended by first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton, Brennan's former high court colleagues and leaders of Congress.
"He loved this country fiercely. He gave himself to it fully. He strengthened it profoundly. And we are all better for it," Clinton said.
He said Brennan became a hero to him as he grew up in Arkansas because of the liberal jurist's civil rights rulings, and that Brennan was "a model for law and service."

The memorial service, featuring hymns and readings from the Bible, took place at St. Matthew's Cathedral, the same Catholic church where the funeral had been held Nov. 25, 1963, for assassinated President John Kennedy.

Clinton listed some of Brennan's rulings that made sure the votes of all Americans have equal weight, that gave free-speech protections to the news media and that broke down barriers of discrimination against women in the workplace.
He said Brennan was one of the few individuals whose ideals helped reshape U.S. history, "saving us from our darker impulses and always pulling us together and pushing us forward."

Justice David Souter, who succeeded Brennan in 1990, said Brennan left behind a legacy in the law that will "transcend his own time." He also recalled how Brennan became his close friend, often embracing Souter with a bear hug.

Souter, who was thought to be a conservative but instead has joined the court's liberal wing, said it was hard to say farewell to Brennan. He repeated what he often said after visiting Brennan at his Supreme Court chambers.
"He'd say, 'So long, pal.' I'd give him a wave. I'd say, 'so long, Bill'."
After the two-hour service also attended by Brennan's family, numerous court employees and friends, Brennan was buried at Arlington National Cemetery in nearby Virginia in a private ceremony.
Brennan, who retired from the bench in 1990 after suffering a stroke, died last week after a long illness. Brennan, 91, had been in failing health for some time.

One of the priests recounted how Brennan in recent years asked for Latin hymns at his funeral, but wanted the service to be joyous. "Remember, I'm Irish," Brennan was quoted as saying. "But for God's sake, keep it short."
